Skylab 2 is the mission that saved America's first space station and, in doing so, proved that astronauts are repair crews as much as explorers. Skylab had reached orbit crippled — its sun shield ripped off during launch, one solar panel gone, the other jammed shut, the interior overheating toward uninhabitable. Pete Conrad's crew flew up to a station that might have been a write-off, deployed a parasol sunshade through a small airlock to cool it, and then freed the stuck panel in a dangerous, improvised spacewalk that restored its power. It was the first time a crew had rescued a failing spacecraft in orbit, and it rewrote the assumption that space hardware was disposable.
First crewed Skylab visit — repaired the damaged workshop and saved the programme

Conrad, Kerwin and Weitz — the first crew to inhabit the US Skylab space station. Launched 1973-05-25 13:00 UTC on Saturn IB (SA-206), 11 days after Skylab itself was damaged at launch (the micrometeoroid / sun shield ripped off, taking one solar wing with it and jamming the second). The crew executed a 28-day rescue: Weitz attempted (and failed) to free the jammed wing during a stand-up EVA of about 40 minutes on day 1, then Conrad and Kerwin successfully cut the restraining strap on a 3.5-hour EVA on day 14, restoring power. Deployed a Marshall-designed parasol thermal shield through the scientific airlock to bring cabin temperatures back from 54°C to 24°C. Returned 1973-06-22 13:50 UTC; CSM-116 displayed at the National Museum of Naval Aviation, Pensacola, Florida.
Saturn IB SA-206 from LC-39B 1973-05-25 13:00 UTC.
CSM docked to Skylab axial port after a soft-dock troubleshoot.
Conrad + Kerwin freed the jammed solar wing during a 3.5h EVA.
CSM-116 splashed down in Pacific 1973-06-22 13:50 UTC.
